[h1]Postal 2: A Hilarious Descent into Madness[/h1]

Ah, "Postal 2" – a game where your daily to-do list can go from “buy milk” to “douse Gary Coleman in gasoline” faster than you can say, “Is this legal?”

The game kicks off innocently enough: you play as The Postal Dude, a man whose only real goal is to get through a week without losing his mind (or causing the apocalypse). Spoiler alert: he fails. Miserably. And hilariously.

Graphics and Sound:
Sure, it looks like it was made in the early 2000s. Probably because it was. But who needs realistic textures when you have rabid elephants and weaponized cats? The sound design is equally unforgettable, with NPCs offering profound insights like, "Get down if you don’t wanna die!” every five seconds. It’s like poetry, but with more obscenities.

Gameplay:
"Postal 2" gives you unparalleled freedom. Want to solve your problems peacefully? Good luck. The game’s AI ensures that even the simplest tasks, like picking up a package, devolve into a bloodbath involving a flamethrower and several dismembered body parts. Your moral compass will spin like a dreidel as you navigate through everyday errands while being chased by a mob of angry protesters and armed police officers. Or maybe that’s just another Tuesday in Postal 2 land.

Weapons and Combat:
This is where "Postal 2" shines like a deranged star. The arsenal ranges from mundane (shovel, scissors) to the utterly absurd (a cow head that spreads mad cow disease). And let’s not forget the cats – both as grenades and silencer attachments. PETA might not approve, but you will.

Story and Missions:
Each day in Postal 2 starts with simple goals: get milk, return a library book, confess your sins. How you accomplish these tasks is entirely up to you. The sheer absurdity of events, like a zombie outbreak at the mall or a Taliban attack, makes for a plot that's both chaotic and weirdly compelling. The mission to get an autograph from Gary Coleman, only to have it turn into a shootout, is particularly legendary. Sorry, Gary.

Social Commentary:
Beneath its crude exterior, Postal 2 is a scathing satire of modern life. It holds a funhouse mirror to our society, highlighting the absurdity of our daily routines and the insanity lurking just beneath the surface. Or maybe it's just a game where you can urinate on people. Who’s to say?

Final Thoughts:
"Postal 2" is a game that laughs in the face of political correctness and decency. It’s like a carnival ride through a madhouse, where every turn brings new horrors and new hilarity. If you’re looking for a game that combines dark humor with wanton destruction, look no further. Just remember, it's only as bad as you are.

Play "Postal 2" – because sometimes, you just need to burn down the neighborhood while screaming incoherently.

Postal 2 is a insane first-person shooter that takes place in Paradise, Arizona, yet it's far from being a paradise.

[h1]The Story[/h1]
In Postal you play as The Postal Dude, a tall thin man with a goatee, sunglasses, a blue alien t-shirt, and a long black leather coat. The story takes place throughout one week. Each day you complete mundane tasks created by your nagging wife. As the days go on the town gets progressively worse with protestors, terrorists, and even the undead.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Gameplay consists of first-person shooting with a handful variety of armaments. The difficulty scales from Liebermode to Really Fucking Hard. On harder difficulties, health items are instantly used on pick-up and civilians will attack on site. This game features secret weapons and ammo giving you an advantage on what's to come. There's a plethora of achievements each consisting of a reference like Loverboy's song [url=http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ahvSgFHzJIc]Everybody's Working for the Weekend[/url] and [url=http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_Family]Modern Family[/url]. Even though this game was created  back in April 13, 2003, the game still gets weekly updates from glorious Running With Scissors, and still can beat today's [i]'next-gen'[/i] games.

The prequel to Animal Crossing (Orig. Doubutsu no Mori, released in 2001 for the Nintendo 64), Postal 2 is an experimental first look at how Animal Crossing would eventually expand. Explore a large, bustling town where each NPC has their own schedule, and you can perform menial-but-fun tasks in any way you wish. 

Featuring many food items, as well as the ability to use the signature 'shovel' item from Animal Crossing, this game has endless possibility for fun. Spend hours gathering all of certain kinds of items, just to say that you did! Fans of Animal Crossing will not be disappointed - I give this game an 11 out of Shigeru Miyamoto.

It's an open world game, based on RWS's brutal dark humor, where throughout the week you have to complete chores or ''errands'', as the game implies, either chaotically or peacefully while each part of the map is unlocked after completing the said day of the week ready to explore and with 15 difficulties to choose from, ranging from ''Liebermode'', the easiest, and ''Impossible'', the hardest, the game only changes a lot of features when you play above the ''Postal'' difficulty, for example, health itens cannot be stored in the inventory and the amount of bullets you can carry gets shortened, while the last example is affected by every difficulty...

There are numerous of features and mechanics included, the AI may not be the best one but sure executes the job right, animals are one of those features, for example, there are dogs who can be useful, if you have dog treats or food, to take down foes while cats, in Zack Ward's style and if you have catnip, are common to be used as both shotgun and M16 silencers. Not to forget to mention,it includes a mechanic detector where it can help you if you are stuck on some corner of the map and weapon spawns changes depending on the day of the week, sometimes you can get more or something different from what you wanted.
Since this game is a Steam version, where it includes ''Share The Pain'', ''Apocalypse Weekend'', ''A Week in Paradise'' and as well a online mode, it supports Steam's Workshop, which until this day is still used by some people.

The design of the map is small with mysterious places and with a creepy atmosphere but sure leaves a certain impression of realism with its inhabitants, without them, it wouldn't be the same...

Achievements? Well, the brutal dark humor from RWS found itself present on the achievements and boy oh boy! What a bunch... Most of them are completely easy, some require items to complete like food or the outfits you can wear but the most difficult one I could do was the ''Anustart!'', complete the main 5 days without killing anyone, with so many weapons and so many victims, it truly was hard for me not to kill anyone! ''Scientology Level: OT VIII'', complete an entire on ''Postal'' difficulty, to be honest, it may be hard at first but when you get the right weapons, it just becomes easier.

[h1] Glitches/Bugs/Error Report: [/h1]

You occasionally may find some bodies and limbs cliping through walls and such or the game crashes when you die too many times or there is too many NPCs for the game to process but that can be fixed in the option menu.

[h1] Overall: [/h1]

Chaotically fascinating and hilarious spending time listenning to Postal Dude's voice lines, I had so much fun playing it and completing everything, while the NPC's made the gameplay more interesting with their shenanigans and the ''Postal'' difficulty was one of the purest experiments to play because it represents the insanity of the game itself, truly would recomend it to somebody who isn't sensitive towards RWS's humor or wants to have the best time of their life, in other words, I regret nothing!

Postal 2.
One of the best games I have ever played in my life.
I mean it serious. I know this game for many years already and played definitely over 300 hours in it (CD & DVD Version). And now it came to Steam. This is the best thing that could have ever happened to it. I bought the game quite often in different editions like the Boxed Edition, Fudge Pack Edition and 10th Anniversary Edition. I also have some other items like a talking Krotchy doll.

Its amazing how much work and heart the developers put into this game.
It still gets updates 12 years after the actual release. Probably the longest supported game in history? Actually it wasnt updated for several years to be honest. It was quite around Postal for many years. Not even Postal 3 changed this fact, especially because it wasnt as good as the most people wanted it to be. It wasnt developed by RWS anyway. I think this game was ok but couldnt reach Postal 2 in any way. I personally do not recommend Postal 3 because its buggy and glitchy as hell. Maybe wait for some proper patches/mods one day...

Now to the actual game review.
In Postal 2 you play as The Postal Dude. One of my favorite game characters of all time. A man living with his wife in a motorhome in the city Paradise.
You have to do normal things like buying stuff in the store or returning books to the mall. Or getting a christmas tree. Those sort of tasks you have to finish to progress in the game.
But this isnt often as easy as we would wish. The crazy city Paradise comes always into our ways. The police, protestors, priests, god*amn even Osama wants us dead. But we can defend ourself and attack back with several weapons. One of the biggest weapon collections ever seen in a game. This Steam versions has even more than the old version. A lot of AWP and ED weapons have been added. Not all but many which doubles the fun. Pistols, shotgun, scissors to rocket launchers. We can also pee on everyone and everything. It was never easier to take a p*ss. Also the gore has been raised extremely. Now you have the same gore amount that was included in the addon Apocalypse Weekend, which is btw included. We can also grab our dog or cat to fight against the citizens but cats are mostly just useful to silence your guns. No, I'm not kidding. There are also other items ingame like "health pipes". Yeah, you know what I mean. In addition to that there are a lot of secrets and goodies ingame! The game is actually open world but with several levels that are only visitable on certain days. Yes the game has days. Monday to Sunday actually. The standard Postal 2 was Monday to Friday but the addon added Saturday and Sunday. You can play Monday to Friday or Saturday and Sunday or the whole week. Everything is possible when you start a new game. Oh and because we came to the start a new game part. There are so many difficulties! I cant remember such a big difficulty amount in any other game. No clue how many exactly there are but definitely over 10! Every of those difficulties offers a different game experience. From the people who hit you with shovels to people who shoot with rocket launchers at you and who are insulted already when you look at them. There is everything. I think that should be enough about the game itself.

The game also has a multiplayer but I think most here wont care for it anyway, its not much played. Its not horrible but kinda outdated, but no wonder. There are still sometimes a few players to find.

The game itself runs with the Unreal Engine 1.5 or 2 when im right. Some hybrid of it.
So it means that this game is dated. If you await nice fancy graphics, you are at the wrong address. But the engine does what is should. It has also been updated with the latest patches released on Steam. Before Steam it was kinda unstable and crashed often. This problems are by now fixed. Also Steamworks has been integrated. Also archievements and trading cards. Workshop exists now too. So everything that a actual game needs, right?
But there are so many fixes and changes by now, that I cant even say them all.
Best to check out the store page. Incredible work by the devs!

Well, what else should I say.
Postal 2 has nothing really to do with Postal 1, yes I played this also.
It was often criticized in the media and banned from a lot of countries due to its gore and seriousness. Doesnt hit everyones taste. I really feel the love the developers put into this game and Postal 2 is between my favorite games of all time. And this game list consists out of Crysis, Fallout etc. I often dare to think about Postal 2 being an Indie game, even if it is. I really love to see this game here on Steam. I bet it will never really die and also todays gamers will always have access to it. It is often on sale for a joke price so definitely a must have! By now there is even a new DLC which adds many hours of new gameplay. I will review this in a seperate review.

I thought Postal 2 was just another ridiculous game where you walk around causing chaos because the developers thought it would be funny.

I was wrong.

The graphics are dated. The gameplay looks chaotic. The world feels completely unhinged.

You start out thinking you're just going to mess around for a few minutes. Then you realize the game is giving you an absurd amount of freedom, and suddenly you're making decisions that no reasonable person would ever make.

The characters are strange. The situations are even stranger. And somehow, every five minutes, the game finds a new way to make you think,

"Wait... did that actually just happen?"

What I love most is that Postal 2 doesn't constantly tell you how you're supposed to play.

It gives you a problem.

Then it gives you an unreasonable number of ways to solve it.

And sometimes the worst possible solution is also the funniest one.

I've played games with better graphics, deeper stories, and much more polished gameplay.

I don't remember most of them.

I'll remember Postal 2.

Some games are fun while you're playing them.

Postal 2 makes you question your life choices while laughing at the absolute insanity happening on screen.

100% recommended.

This game is peak, and I say that after 16 hours of playing and finishing 2 full playthroughs of Postal 2. I went into it expecting a simple shock value game from the early 2000s, but after spending real time with it I can say it is the best fucking game I have ever played. Postal 2 drops you into the town of Paradise with a basic goal for each day of the week, and that goal sounds simple on paper. You need to buy milk, return a library book, pick up a paycheck, or grab something from a store. The design sounds small, but the freedom you get while doing these tasks is huge. The map is open, connected, and full of people who react to what you do. You walk down the street and hear random conversations, arguments, and complaints. NPCs talk about politics, religion, work, and everyday problems. Some insult you, some ignore you, and some panic the moment things get chaotic. The result feels alive. The game does not force you into a strict path. You choose how each task plays out. You can walk calmly to the store, stand in line, and leave without trouble. You can also lose patience, start a fight, and turn the entire street into a disaster. Both options work, and the game reacts to them in ways that make each moment feel different. The humor is crude and aggressive, but it lands because the game commits to it fully. Every location adds something memorable. The police station feels tense because officers react fast if you cause problems. The church turns into chaos if you push things too far. The grocery store feels normal until one small decision makes the entire place collapse into shouting and panic. This constant tension makes even simple errands exciting. The controls are simple and direct. Movement feels responsive and quick. Shooting feels solid for a game of its age. You pick up weapons easily and understand how they work within seconds. The arsenal grows as the week progresses, and each weapon adds a different style of play. Some weapons cause loud and fast destruction. Others create slower chaos that spreads through crowds and streets. The variety keeps the experience fresh across the entire campaign. What surprised me most is how much the game rewards experimentation. I tried one approach in my first playthrough and a completely different approach in my second. The results felt like two separate games. In the first run I played cautiously. I avoided fights, followed tasks directly, and tried to keep the police away from me. That run still created many unpredictable moments because the town reacts to small actions. A random insult from an NPC can start a chain reaction that spreads across the street. A protest group might block your path. A single mistake can trigger alarms and police chases. In the second playthrough I decided to push the systems harder. I interacted with more NPCs, explored side paths, and triggered more events on purpose. The world responded with louder reactions, larger fights, and constant tension with the police. This flexibility is why the game holds attention for long sessions. After 16 hours I still found new interactions and hidden jokes. The writing plays a big role in that replay value. Dialogue sounds blunt and direct, which fits the tone of the game. Characters express frustration, anger, and sarcasm in ways that feel raw instead of polished. Many lines still get a laugh because they come out of nowhere during normal gameplay. One moment you walk quietly through a street. The next moment someone starts yelling about something ridiculous and the situation spirals from there. The main character also adds personality to the experience. His reactions to events feel casual and irritated, which fits the constant problems he faces while trying to finish simple errands. The soundtrack supports the mood without getting in the way. Music appears during tense moments and fades during exploration. Sound effects carry most of the atmosphere. You hear distant sirens, crowds shouting, dogs barking, and doors slamming. These details make the town feel active even when you stand still. The map layout deserves credit because it encourages exploration. Streets loop around each other and connect through alleys, parks, and buildings. You often discover shortcuts after several hours that change how you move through the town. That discovery process makes later days faster and more strategic. Enemy reactions also improve the tension. Police arrive quickly when violence starts, and they escalate their response if you keep causing trouble. Civilians run, scream, or fight back depending on the situation. Groups react differently from individuals. A single NPC might panic and flee. A crowd might surround you and shout until the situation explodes. These reactions create many unpredictable encounters. Performance holds up well during large fights and busy streets. Even when many characters appear on screen the game remains playable and clear. Visual quality reflects the era it came from, but the art style keeps environments readable. Buildings, stores, and public areas stand out enough that you always know where you are. Paradise feels like a strange version of a real town. Each district adds its own tone. Some areas feel quiet and normal. Others feel unstable the moment you enter them. This variety prevents the game from becoming repetitive. Each day introduces new tasks and locations that push you into different corners of the map. The pacing also works well. Tasks remain short enough that you never feel stuck in one objective for too long. At the same time the game allows long sessions because every trip across the map can turn into a new situation. During my 16 hours I had many moments where I planned to finish one quick errand and stop playing, but the trip created three new problems and I kept going for another hour. Few games manage that kind of pull. Postal 2 does it through simple systems that interact in unpredictable ways. The shock value often gets the most attention when people talk about this game, but the real strength comes from the freedom and the reactions of the world around you. Every system connects to the others. Movement, weapons, NPC behavior, police response, and map design all support the same idea. You enter the town, choose your approach, and deal with the results. That design creates stories that feel personal because you caused them through your decisions. After two full playthroughs I still think about moments where things went wrong or turned into chaos in unexpected ways. Few games stay that memorable after only 16 hours. Postal 2 does it through confident design and complete commitment to its tone. The game knows exactly what it wants to be and never pulls back from that direction. That confidence makes the experience stand out even today. Many modern games chase massive worlds and endless content but forget to give players meaningful freedom. Postal 2 proves that a smaller world with strong reactions can create far more memorable gameplay. After finishing it twice I feel confident saying it stands above every other game I have played. It delivers freedom, humor, tension, and replay value in a way that still feels fresh. For me it is the best fucking game I have ever played, and after 16 hours and two full playthroughs I still want to start another run just to see what kind of chaos Postal 2 throws back at me next.

"If you like violence and comedy, this game is perfect for you."

This sort of game is dangerous. Not because of its juvenile and offensive sense of humor (which I personally feel has aged like fine wine in the internet age), or because of the fact you can kill pretty much everyone and everything including in game representations of the game developers themselves; no. What's dangerous about Postal 2 is how gosh darn easy it is to spend all your time playing this thing as if time were currency and the game was that Terminator Salvation cabinet at the bowling alley that you know you'd spend all your parents life's earnings on were there ever a space a mile-long line for you. 

What's so fantastic about Postal 2 isn't necessarily the gameplay itself, rather what sets it apart is the amount of choice you have while playing it. In fact as I'm sure plenty have either made sure to point out or completely ignore (given the type of person they are) that it is entirely possible to beat the game without any violence on your part. Now, I feel obligated to say that it's not easy by any means, definitely not (unless you play on the lowest difficulty wherein most range weapons are replaced with blunt melee weapons). The townspeople in this town are arguably equally if not more psychotic than the protagonist is implied to be, so beating it without any violence whatsoever is a challenge to be sure, but the fact its an option at all is just a testament to the sort of game we're dealing with here. This versatility combined with the relatively simple gameplay loop of doing mundane tasks and getting attacked by psychotic townspeople makes more an almost endlessly re-playable experience. I always want to try things in different ways to see how they pan out, create little challenges for myself. For instance; do I go into the bank guns blazing or do I steal a cop uniform and sneak in that way? Should I just wait in line and cash my paycheck like a normal person? The choice is yours!

The game has been updated a lot since the original version back in 2003. To my understanding they've added weapons from both the Apocalypse Weekend expansion and some fan mods into the base game. Some range from pure novelty to full on balance shattering, but that balancing thing never becomes an issue as weapons like this and their ammunition are almost always hidden and require some sleuthing or just a keen eye to find. Speaking of which, there are lots of secrets to find as well. Paradise is a very sprawling environment (which is probably my one complaint, navigation can be a nightmare, though part of me thinks this is intentional),and with it being so large I still feel like there's plenty I'm probably missing. Even with its janky aspects here and there you can just feel the amount of care that went into this game, including even its irreverent and satirical sense of humor. 

Running With Scissors have definitely earned their longevity after all these years. They very clearly put a lot of care into this as well as their other projects and are very responsive to any questions or issues people seem to have, frequently making a conscious effort to involve the community in their efforts to improve their products. As a consumer I find this admirable on so many levels. It's so funny how a series known by most outsiders as the most offensive thing ever is made by a bunch of potty mouthed sweethearts. Take my heart RWS, you earned it.

The game comes with the more linear but (in my opinion) equally as enjoyable Apocalypse Weekend expansion right out of the box, the 11 years "late" Paradise Lost DLC is cheap and essentially a whole fully fledged game on its own, and it even runs like butter on my Macbook Pro. There's honestly no reason [i]not[/i] to play it unless you can't stomach the crude humor or gore.

So yeah, here's my most glowing of recommendations to the self proclaimed "Worst Game Ever Made" as one of the most genuinely fun experiences I've had with a game in a long time. "Check it out or I'll follow you home and kill your dog."

but in all seriousness though, this game is fantastic and it all comes down to how the gameplay and tone mix with each other.
the gameplay is, in simple terms, the deranged sickly child of a loot-all-the-corners, objective-grabbing, backtracking boomer shooter, and a go anywhere, fully intractable, dynamic sandbox game. the world is full of secrets, collectibles, easter eggs, weapons, secret areas, unique enemy encounters, and funny vent secrets that give you the most overpowered weapon in the game (GO TO THE MALL ON THURSDAY). but instead of the thing that like all AAA games do nowadays where they mark every single nick-knack on the map and then give you 1 main mission, postal 2 does the exact opposite. the ONLY things that are marked on your map are the current day's errands. because this game gives you multiple story areas and lets you go to them in whatever order you like. and, last but not least, the best part of the gameplay, [b]postal 2 takes place over the course of a week.[/b] every day, all of the secrets and stuff get either reset, or replaced with better secrets. and each day more of the map opens up. so you start a routine, you start repeating yourself. and then, when your schedule finally clicks into place, and everything lines up, and its friday, the game throws a curveball at you that i refuse to spoil. then after that (assuming you are playing the full week mode, monday-sunday) you get put into apocolypse weekend and the game (temporarily) turns into a sub-par linear game that, while not as good as the base game, is a good change of pace and refreshes the experience.

the tone is: literally an ultra-parody of life itself. every single viewpoint that could exist is made fun of, puked on, and then the people making fun of it are made fun of. aside from the game taking the piss out of literally every political and moral standpoint that could ever exist, the game is intentionally disgusting. its so disgusting, gory, edgy and awful, but it doesn't take itself seriously at all, so it never comes off as nihilistic. its just like, "yeah everything sucks and the world is a terrible awful place, but haha piss button lol" oh yeah you get a piss button in this game. you can piss on anything.

now for an example of how the gameplay and the tone work together: you get set on fire ALOT in this game. be it from enemies, accidentally setting yourself on fire, or both, its impossible to play this game without getting set on fire. well then how do you extinguish yourself? how do you mitigate the damage?

remember the piss button?

[b]you piss on yourself to extinguish the flames.[/b]

Postal 2 is that game that is somehow greater than the sum of its parts. It's old, clunky, ugly as sin, offensive just for the sake of being offensive, and yet there's a certain South Park sort of spectrum of hilarity to it.

That and it's still being kept up to date 13 years later, including the release of a whole new expansion. Where else are you going to find that?
